questions.stem: An account pays a nominal annual interest rate of 4.8%, compounded monthly. Deposits of 800 dollars are made at the end of every month for 10 years. The initial balance is zero. Annual inflation is assumed to remain at 2.5%. Ignore tax and fees.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write down the monthly interest rate as a decimal.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the balance immediately after the 120th deposit.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Express that balance in today's purchasing power.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Find the monthly deposit required to achieve purchasing power of 100 000 dollars after 10 years, under the same assumptions.

steps.text: Divide by $1.025^{10}$, giving $96013.633$ dollars in today's money.
Set the target future balance to $100000(1.025)^{10}$ and solve for the deposit.
The required deposit is $833.21501$ dollars per month (round up to the next cent if an attainable minimum payment is required).

questions.stem: A chemical sensor has response $S(c)=(18c+12)/(c+4)$ mV at concentration $c\ge0$ mg L$^{-1}$. The response is increasing on this physical domain.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find $c$ as a function of $S$, and state the physical domain of this inverse.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the concentration corresponding to 14 mV.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the concentration changes corresponding to signal increases from 13 to 14 mV and from 15 to 16 mV. Explain what this says about sensitivity at high concentration.

steps.text: The inverse domain is $3\le S<18$, since $S(0)=3$ and the response approaches 18 from below.
The concentration changes are $11-8=3$ and $26-16=10$ mg L$^{-1}$ respectively.
A larger concentration change gives the same 1 mV response change at high concentration; the sensor is less sensitive there.

questions.stem:
Seven hikers report their weekly training distance $x$ (km) and the time $y$ (minutes) to complete a steep climb.

| Hiker | A | B | C | D | E | F | G |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | 12 | 14 | 14 | 18 | 20 | 23 | 25 |
| $y$ | 44 | 40 | 42 | 35 | 37 | 31 | 28 |

Rank both variables in ascending order, using average ranks for ties.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write down the rank lists for $x$ and $y$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Interpret the sign and magnitude of this coefficient. State why it does not by itself prove that training causes a faster climb.

steps.text: Calculate the Pearson correlation of the rank lists, which handles the tied ranks.
There is a strong negative monotonic association: greater training distance tends to be associated with shorter climb times.
The data are observational and may be confounded, for example by baseline fitness or age; correlation is not proof of causation.

questions.stem: A robot must inspect every corridor in the undirected network at least once and return to its starting station A. Edge labels are corridor lengths in metres. It may repeat corridors; crossings away from labelled stations are not junctions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why traversing every corridor exactly once in a closed route is impossible.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the minimum total length of corridors that must be repeated.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the minimum length of a complete inspection route and explain why your construction permits a closed route.

steps.text: Vertices A,B,C,D have odd degree 3. A connected graph admits an Euler circuit only when all degrees are even.
Pair the four odd vertices using shortest path distances.
The three pairing totals are $7, 17, 11$ m.
Repeat AB and CD, for $7$ m in total.
The original edge total is $40$ m.
The minimum route length is $40+7=47$ m.
Duplicating the selected paths makes every vertex even while preserving connectivity, so an Euler circuit of that length exists.

questions.stem: A factory claims that a new process reduces the defect probability from 0.20. Thirty independent items are tested and two are defective. Use a one-tailed exact binomial test at the 5% level. For a lower-tail critical region, choose the largest rejection probability strictly below 0.05.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the hypotheses for the new defect probability $p$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the $p$-value and state the test decision.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the critical region, showing that the next larger lower-tail region is not permitted.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Find the probability of a Type II error when the true defect probability is 0.10.

steps.text: $p=0.044178985<0.05$; reject the null hypothesis in favour of a reduction.
$P_0(X\le 3)=0.12271081>0.05$, so the region cannot be enlarged.
Failing to reject means $X>2$, now with $X\sim B(30,0.10)$.
The Type II error probability is $0.58864876$.

questions.stem:
Nine independent observations of the lifetime of a component, in hours, are

$42.1,44.8,41.7,46.3,43.5,45.2,42.9,44.1,43.7$.

Assume a random sample from a normal population whose variance is unknown.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the sample mean and unbiased sample standard deviation.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find a 95% confidence interval for the population mean lifetime.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Comment on a claimed mean lifetime of 44.5 hours, and explain why the interval is not a range containing 95% of individual lifetimes.

steps.text: Use a $t$ interval with $df=8$, not the population standard deviation.
44.5 hours lies inside this interval, so this sample is compatible with that mean at this confidence level.
The interval estimates the population mean using the standard error; it is not a prediction interval for individual observations.

questions.stem:
The cross-sectional area $A(x)$ of a flooded tunnel is measured perpendicular to its axis at equally spaced positions.

| $x$ / m | 0 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 | 100 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $A(x)$ / m$^2$ | 0 | 18 | 29 | 25 | 14 | 0 |

Assume $A(x)$ is continuous and strictly concave down between the ends.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the trapezoidal rule with intervals of width 20 m to estimate the water volume.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Additional areas at $x=10,30,50,70,90$ are respectively $9.5,24,28.5,20,7.5$ m$^2$. Find the trapezoidal estimate using width 10 m.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the concavity assumption, state whether these trapezoidal estimates are underestimates or overestimates, and justify your answer.

questions.answerSummary: T20=1720.0m³;T10=1755.0m³; both underestimate under stated concavity.

steps.text: Interleave all eleven equally spaced observations; endpoints are zero.
Each chord lies below a concave-down graph.
The trapezoids therefore underestimate the integral and hence the volume; the larger refined estimate is consistent with this.

questions.stem: A two-stage population has juvenile and adult state vector $\mathbf s_n$. It follows $\mathbf s_{n+1}=L\mathbf s_n$, where $L=\begin{pmatrix}0&1.8\\0.5&0.3\end{pmatrix}$. Initially there are 200 juveniles and 100 adults. Fractional population predictions are permitted within the model.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the predicted juvenile and adult populations one year later.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the dominant eigenvalue and interpret its long-run growth implication.

parts.label: c

steps.text: The eigenvalues are $1.1104686$ and $-0.81046864$; the dominant magnitude is $1.1104686$.
The model eventually grows by a factor $1.1104686$ per year, about $11.05\%$ annually.

questions.stem:
A courier must start at A, visit each of B,C,D,E once, and return to A. The complete undirected distance table, in kilometres, is shown.

|  | A | B | C | D | E |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | — | 6 | 9 | 10 | 7 |
| B | 6 | — | 5 | 8 | 9 |
| C | 9 | 5 | — | 6 | 8 |
| D | 10 | 8 | 6 | — | 4 |
| E | 7 | 9 | 8 | 4 | — |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Apply the nearest-neighbour algorithm starting at A. State the resulting tour and an upper bound for the optimum.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the deleted-vertex method, deleting A, to obtain a lower bound.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the optimal tour length and justify your conclusion.

steps.text: Choose the closest unvisited vertex at each step.
Its length is $6+5+6+4+7=28$ km, an upper bound.
A minimum spanning tree on B,C,D,E uses DE,BC,CD.
Add the two smallest A-edges, 6 and 7, to obtain a lower bound of $28$ km.
The lower and upper bounds are equal.
The optimum is exactly $28$ km; the tour in part (a) attains it.

questions.stem: An object initially at $90^\circ$C cools according to $dT/dt=-0.15(T-A)$, where $t$ is minutes and $A$ is ambient temperature. For $0\le t<4$, $A=20$. parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the first time after $t=0$ at which the temperature reaches $15^\circ$C.

parts.prompt: Find the cooling rates immediately before and after the move, and explain why the derivative changes even though temperature is continuous.

steps.text: The rates are $-5.7625222$ and $-8.0125222^\circ$C min$^{-1}$ respectively.
The ambient temperature changes by 15 degrees, changing the derivative by $-0.15(15)=-2.25$ degrees per minute.
The driving temperature difference changes immediately, while the object's temperature does not jump.
